p: Knole's owners read like a who's who of English history. Thomas Bourchier, Archbishop of Canterbury, bought the estate in the fifteenth century and built much of the palace. Henry VIII later took it for himself, and Elizabeth I gave it to her cousin Thomas Sackville, whose family have been linked with it ever since. The writer Vita Sackville-West grew up here, and her friend Virginia Woolf drew on Knole and the family's history for her novel Orlando. Book lovers, this one's for you.

There's an old story that Knole is a calendar house, with 365 rooms, 52 staircases and 12 entrances, matching the days, weeks and months of the year. Whether it adds up exactly is hard to say, but it gives you a sense of the scale, and it's a fun one to test the kids with.

Out in the park, the deer are the stars. Both fallow and sika deer roam freely, and they can be very used to people. Admire them, but don't feed them, and keep your distance, especially in autumn during the rut and in early summer when they have young.

Allow at least half a day for house and park. Sevenoaks station is roughly a fifteen- to twenty-minute walk away. Nearby, Ightham Mote is a wonderful moated medieval manor, and Chartwell, Winston Churchill's family home near Westerham, makes a great second day out. Hever Castle, childhood home of Anne Boleyn, is within easy reach too.
